Graph key
Tempo & accumulated beats
Red: elapsed beats (Ë) from the approximate pulse
Dashed gray: elapsed beats at one steady BPM (the BPM shown)
Gray-brown: approximate local BPM over about eight beat intervals
Swing, arpeggios and individual notes can move around a steady pulse. The local reading averages those timings while retaining slower drift, expressive rubato and section changes. Eight beats are not always two bars. Flatness alone cannot identify a click track.
Red integrates BPM ÷ 60 over time: Ë is an approximate accumulated pulse count, not an exact annotation of every beat. Dotted tempo shows an approximate fluctuation reading; Change reports movement on that same graph. Unmetered music may have no single meaningful BPM. A listed BPM sets the displayed reference; the curve follows this recording.
BPM values sit on the left edge; Ë counts sit above the time labels. The Change meter follows the gray-brown line. Click or tap to position; drag to scrub.

About these readings

Averages are weighted by play count; a plain song list counts each song once. Each column has its own range. Select a column to see its full readout. The Ë column uses hundreds of beats: 2 means 200 Ë.

Ë uses an imported beat count or the analyzed song curve when available; otherwise it is calculated from song duration × BPM ÷ 60. The BPM scale is 40–300; Ë, time and fluctuation start at 0 and expand for larger values. Genre uses a fixed low-to-high energy ordering for the white bar; the genre name itself is still chosen by your play counts.

Approx. BPM fluctuation uses the time-weighted mean absolute deviation around an analyzed song's mean BPM. Before audio analysis, database/profile songs can use a conservative estimate anchored to the best known or community-corrected BPM plus available metadata; real audio analysis replaces that estimate. The last VFD character shows the reading’s actual + or − sign.

Genre comes from supplied song metadata. Readings use songs with the required data; coverage appears above. Import BPM, duration and genre data, or analyze matching songs in the Player, to fill missing readings.

About this catalogue & BPM corrections
Tap a row to highlight it; tap the same row again to deselect it. Database selection never changes Manual BPM Override or the digital BPM display. Online search can pull large result sets without loading their BPM into the player; online rows can be BPM-corrected on any device and then become Learned. Rows marked Verified were measured in this browser from the decoded file; Learned rows contain a saved correction; Reference rows are published values. Double-click a BPM with a mouse/trackpad to edit it. On phones and other touch devices, press and hold the BPM value to edit. Corrections sync through the cloud so the newest saved BPM is available on your other devices too. This never changes the digital BPM display.

4D Spatial Field
Studio spatial rendering — the mix plays exactly as recorded; the stage widens and the room opens around it.

4D opens the stereo image out of your head without changing the mix. A mid/side stage keeps the bass mono and tight, gently widens the sides and adds a subtle speaker-style crossfeed, so the music sits in front of and around you instead of in one spot. A short, damped room adds natural depth at a low level, and only the recording's own ambience (its side content) is spread to the sides, rear and above — vocals and the centre stay dry and precise. Nothing moves, pans, swirls or gets remixed; tempo and pitch are untouched, and loudness is matched to the original. Headphones recommended. Turning 4D off restores the original signal exactly.
